abstract: >-
  Most EEG source imaging methods assume brain activity arises from independent, focal sources and are validated mainly on their ability to localize a single generator, overlooking the brain's network structure and the co-activation of regions along it. We introduce weighted Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (wCSET), which replaces its predecessor CSET's L1 sparsity prior with a smooth, exponentially weighted L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum. We validate wCSET, CSET, three standard connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based alternative (GBF) across three complementary studies that probe source reconstruction beyond localization. The first simulates activity propagating across a structural connectome, providing an exact network-level ground truth. The second uses a clinical cohort of 26 seizure-free patients with epilepsy, with the resected volume as ground truth. The third uses simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG recordings, a rare direct electrophysiological benchmark. In simulation, wCSET matched standard methods at localizing a source's onset but substantially outperformed them at reconstructing the distributed co-activation patterns that follow as activity spreads, an advantage robust to moderate noise and to considerable connectome corruption. In the resection cohort, wCSET's localization did not differ significantly from any other method. Against intracranial recordings, wCSET outperformed the standard methods and CSET in one of two evaluable subjects on two polarity-invariant measures, and did not differ from them in the other. A purely geometric alternative matched wCSET's own performance throughout, suggesting cortical geometry alone may capture much of what drives accurate distributed reconstruction. Together, these results establish wCSET as a principled step beyond localization-only source imaging, and introduce a validation framework for evaluating such methods against a source's full co-activation pattern rather than its location alone.

# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity non-invasively with millisecond resolution, but volume conduction through the skull and scalp limits its spatial resolution, so each electrode records a mixture of activity from a large cortical area [@nunez_electric_2006]. Source reconstruction (also known as source imaging) estimates the underlying cortical activity from these recordings [@hamalainen_interpreting_1994; @dale_improved_1993]. This inverse problem, however, is ill-posed. Because infinitely many source configurations explain the same scalp data, every method must constrain the solution with prior assumptions [@knosche_eegmeg_2022; @wipf_unified_2009].

Distributed source models differ mainly in these prior assumptions. They represent cortical activity as a dense set of dipoles [@dale_improved_1993] and constrain how the source amplitudes are distributed. Minimum-norm methods, namely MNE [@hamalainen_interpreting_1994] and its weighted or normalized variants dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002] and eLORETA [@pascual-marqui_discrete_2007], penalize the L2 norm of the source amplitudes. In a Bayesian framework, this penalty corresponds to a Gaussian prior on independent sources and yields spatially diffuse estimates [@wipf_unified_2009]. Penalizing the L1 norm instead, as in the minimum current estimate (MCE) [@uutela_visualization_1999], corresponds to a Laplace prior on independent sources and yields sparse, focal estimates [@wipf_unified_2009]. Both families therefore assume that sources are independent a priori, a choice made for mathematical simplicity rather than physiological realism. The brain, however, operates as an integrated network of co-active regions [@bressler_large-scale_2010], and priors that treat each source independently ignore the structure that links them.

This structure can be encoded in the prior itself. In the Gaussian Bayesian framework, the prior source covariance matrix describes how sources co-vary [@wipf_unified_2009]. Its diagonal entries set the expected power of each source, and its off-diagonal entries encode co-activation between sources. Priors that encode co-activation can reduce source leakage [@schoffelen_source_2009; @gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018], and methods that use them differ mainly in where this off-diagonal structure comes from. Proximity-based methods link neighboring sources: LORETA imposes spatial smoothness through a discrete Laplacian operator [@pascual-marqui_low_1994], and LAURA through local autoregressive averages [@grave_de_peralta_menendez_noninvasive_2001]. fMRI-informed methods use spatial priors derived from fMRI [@liu_fmri-si-stbf_2021]. Data-driven methods, such as BC-VARETA [@gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018; @gonzalez-moreira_third_2018], estimate the source covariance jointly with the source activity. Each of these sources of structure has limits. Proximity priors ignore long-range connections, fMRI priors reflect slow hemodynamic coupling rather than fast electrical coupling [@liu_fmri-si-stbf_2021], and data-driven methods must estimate many additional parameters from data that already underdetermine the sources.

The structural connectome offers a fourth source of structure. It combines long-range white-matter connections, reconstructed from diffusion MRI by tractography, with short-range connections within gray matter [@atasoy_human_2016; @ruequeralt_connectome_2024]. This network captures the long-range links that proximity priors miss, reflects anatomy rather than hemodynamics, and adds no parameters to estimate from the EEG. Recent work on structure–function coupling shows that the eigenvectors of the connectome's graph Laplacian, known as connectome harmonics, define a graph Fourier basis for brain activity [@shuman_emerging_2013; @atasoy_human_2016; @huang_graph_2016], and that brain activity concentrates in a few low-frequency harmonics [@atasoy_human_2016; @rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) builds on this basis [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024]. It applies a sparse prior to the graph Fourier coefficients of the source activity, so that the reconstructed activity is represented by a small number of connectome harmonics.

Other methods apply the same graph Fourier approach to the cortical surface instead of the connectome [@siu_structural_2026; @wang_geometry_2026]. They replace the connectome's graph Laplacian with the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the cortical mesh, whose eigenvectors, known as geometric harmonics, explain brain activity about as well as connectome harmonics in the structure–function coupling literature [@mansour_eigenmodes_2024]. Geometric harmonics require only the T1-weighted image [@pang_geometric_2023], which subject-level source reconstruction already uses to build the head model, but they ignore the long-range white-matter connections that the connectome captures. The most recent of these methods, Geometric Basis Functions (GBF) [@wang_geometry_2026], places a Gaussian prior on the graph Fourier coefficients and assigns each harmonic a weight, the prior standard deviation of its coefficient. A structure–function coupling study reports that the spectrum of brain activity decays exponentially with harmonic frequency [@abdelnour_functional_2018]. GBF's authors tested exponentially decaying weights but chose, empirically, logarithmically decaying weights truncated after the first 300 harmonics. Unlike CSET's sparse prior, these weights explicitly favour low-frequency harmonics, so the reconstructed spectrum concentrates in the low-frequency range, as observed experimentally [@atasoy_human_2016; @rue-queralt_connectome_2021].

We propose weighted CSET, which combines the connectome harmonics of CSET with the harmonic weighting of GBF. Weighted CSET places a Gaussian prior on the graph Fourier coefficients of the connectome harmonics, with harmonic weights that decay exponentially with harmonic frequency. The reconstructed spectrum therefore follows the exponential decay reported in this structure–function coupling study [@abdelnour_functional_2018].

Evaluating such connectivity-informed methods, which model co-activation between sources, requires different benchmarks. Most methods are evaluated on how accurately they recover the location and extent of a source [@grova_evaluation_2006; @carboni_linear_2022], metrics that assume brain activity consists of focal sources. For a focal source, however, the independence assumption holds, because the source has no co-active regions to model. Localization benchmarks therefore cannot reveal what connectivity-informed priors add. We hypothesize that these priors bring little benefit for localizing a source at its onset but improve the reconstruction of activity after onset, as it propagates through the cortex.

Testing this hypothesis is difficult because no single benchmark provides a complete ground truth for co-activation: simulations are exact but idealized, surgical resections are clinically grounded but spatially coarse, and intracranial EEG (iEEG) is direct but sparsely sampled. We therefore combine three complementary studies, each comparing CSET and weighted CSET (wCSET) with standard methods:

-   **Study I (simulations).** We simulate activity propagating across the structural connectome, which provides an exact and fully known ground truth for co-activation that no recording can offer. We test whether connectivity-informed methods reconstruct the co-activation patterns that follow a source's onset, and how robust they are to errors in the connectome.

-   **Study II (epilepsy surgery).** In a clinical epilepsy cohort, the resected zone serves as the reference, and seizure freedom after surgery confirms that it contained the epileptogenic source [@rosenow_presurgical_2001; @carboni_linear_2022; @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020]. We test whether connectivity-informed methods localize this source as accurately as standard methods.

-   **Study III (simultaneous EEG–iEEG).** As a proof of concept in a small cohort, we use simultaneous scalp EEG and iEEG recordings, following the framework of @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026, who compared magnetoencephalography (MEG) source reconstructions with iEEG. iEEG provides a direct electrophysiological reference, free from neurovascular coupling, skull attenuation and temporal blurring [@nunez_electric_2006]. By projecting the EEG reconstructions onto the iEEG electrode locations, we compare reconstructed and recorded co-activation patterns at each time point.

Together, these studies form a multi-level evaluation framework that moves the evaluation of source reconstruction beyond localization alone.

# Materials and Methods

We evaluate wCSET in three complementary studies (@fig-overview). All three reconstruct the EEG with the same pipeline and compare the same six methods: three minimum-norm baselines that assume independent sources (wMNE, dSPM and sLORETA), the geometry-based method GBF, and the two connectome-based methods CSET and wCSET. This section describes, in turn, the shared pipeline (@sec-pipeline), the datasets and their study-specific settings (@sec-datasets), the metrics that compare each reconstruction with its study's reference (the simulated activity, the resected zone or the iEEG recordings) (@sec-metrics), and the statistical analysis (@sec-stats).

![*Shared reconstruction pipeline and three complementary validation studies.* Top: all studies reconstruct the EEG with the same pipeline. Red marks brain activity; green marks the reference against which each reconstruction is evaluated. **Study I (left), simulations:** activity propagates from a focal source across the structural connectome. Each reconstruction is compared with the simulated activity by spatial correlation over time; the example shows wCSET and sLORETA at onset (t₁) and after propagation (t₂). Onset localization is evaluated separately (@sec-metric-loc). **Study II (middle), epilepsy surgery:** in patients seizure-free after surgery, localization error is the Euclidean distance between the peak of the reconstructed activity and the resected zone (0 mm if the peak lies inside it). **Study III (right), simultaneous EEG–iEEG:** reconstructions are projected onto the intracranial contacts ("virtual iEEG") and compared with the recorded iEEG by the rank correlation of amplitudes and the area under the ROC curve (AUC) across contacts.](results/overview_method.png){#fig-overview fig-alt="Schematic of the shared source reconstruction pipeline (MRI and electrode positions, source space, forward model, connectome and harmonics, inverse solution, reconstructed activity) branching into three study panels: simulation with ground-truth and reconstructed brain maps at two time points, resection cohort with the distance between estimated location and resection volume, and simultaneous EEG/iEEG with reconstructed sources projected onto intracranial electrodes."}

## Source Reconstruction Pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

### Source Space {#sec-source-space}

We modeled neural activity with a distributed dipole model constrained to the cortex. For each subject, MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013] placed about 7,500 dipoles on the white-matter surface reconstructed with FreeSurfer from the T1-weighted MRI. The dipoles have a mean spacing of 3.3 mm and a fixed orientation normal to the surface (@sec-annex-source).

<!-- What moved to the Annex: the exact dipole range, the FreeSurfer version, the subdivision scheme and the rationale for fixed orientations. The paragraph went from 4 sentences to 3 and keeps every decision that matters for interpreting the results. The last sentence ends on the two properties that later sections rely on, spacing and orientation -->

### Volume Conduction Model {#sec-bem}

For each subject, we built a three-layer head model from the T1-weighted MRI with a custom pipeline based on SimNIBS CHARM [@puonti_accurate_2020], which extracts non-intersecting inner-skull, outer-skull and scalp surfaces (@sec-annex-bem). Treating these surfaces as boundaries between compartments of homogeneous conductivity, we modeled volume conduction with the boundary element method (BEM) [@hamalainen_realistic_1989], using MNE-Python's default conductivities of 0.3 S/m for brain and scalp and 0.006 S/m for skull. In the clinical studies (@sec-data-resection, @sec-data-ieeg), the EEG electrode positions were already co-registered to the T1-weighted MRI and therefore aligned with the head model. In the simulation study (@sec-data-synthetic), we projected a template EEG montage onto the scalp surface. Finally, MNE-Python computed the forward solution, the gain matrix that maps source activity to the EEG electrodes.

<!-- What moved to the Annex: fitting of surfaces implementation detail, BEM comparison -->

### Structural Connectome and Graph Harmonics {#sec-connectome}

CSET and wCSET compute their harmonics from a structural connectome defined on the source space. We represent this connectome as a weighted graph whose nodes are the source-space dipoles and whose edges are anatomical connections between them. Only Study I includes diffusion MRI, for its single subject from the VEPCON dataset (@sec-data-synthetic), so only Study I uses an individual connectome. Studies II and III use an atlas surrogate, chosen because it performs comparably to the other surrogates in Study I while retaining long-range white-matter connections.

**Individual connectome**

The connectome combines two types of edges. Long-range edges are white-matter connections reconstructed from diffusion MRI by tractography. Short-range edges link each dipole to all dipoles within a fixed geodesic distance and capture the local connectivity within gray matter that tractography misses. Unlike the mesh Laplacian of LORETA, which links only adjacent grid points with equal weights, these short-range edges span a geodesic radius and are weighted by distance. Each edge is weighted by its length: the fiber length for long-range edges and the geodesic distance for short-range edges (@sec-annex-connectome).

**Connectome surrogates**

When diffusion MRI is unavailable, a surrogate must replace the individual connectome. Study I (@sec-study1) evaluates three surrogates, each testing which part of the connectome the reconstructions depend on (@tbl-surrogates). To separate the graph's topology from its edge weights, we also test the atlas and local surrogates in binarized form, with all edges weighted equally, which gives five variants in total. The geometric surrogate is the GBF method as published: it replaces both the connectome harmonics with geometric harmonics and wCSET's exponential weights with GBF's logarithmic weights. Because GBF differs from wCSET in both the harmonics and the weights, a difference in their performance cannot be attributed to either one alone.

| Surrogate | Construction | Binarized variant | Tests whether… |
|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------:|:----------------|
| Atlas | Long-range edges from the multi-scale connectivity (MultiConn) atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], a probabilistic population atlas of the structural connectome (scale 4), plus the short-range edges above | Yes | a population atlas can replace individual tractography |
| Local | Short-range edges only, plus homotopic links between hemispheres to keep the graph connected | Yes | short-range connections suffice without long-range ones |
| Geometric (GBF) | No graph; geometric harmonics of the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the cortical mesh [@pang_geometric_2023], with GBF's logarithmic weights truncated after 300 harmonics | No (no graph to binarize) | the existing geometric approach matches connectome-based reconstruction |

: Connectome surrogates evaluated in Study I. Construction details are given in @sec-annex-connectome. {#tbl-surrogates}

**Graph Fourier transform**

<!-- To add in annex: We used inverse-distance weights for simplicity; since binarized connectomes perform as well as weighted ones (@sec-results-surrogates), the choice of weighting function is unlikely to affect the results. -->

Because edge weights are lengths, we invert them to obtain an adjacency matrix $\mathbf A$ whose entries describe connection strength, so that shorter connections couple more strongly, in line with the decay of connection strength with distance [@ercsey-ravasz_predictive_2013]. From $\mathbf A$, we build the normalized graph Laplacian

$$
\mathcal L = \mathbf I - \mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2},
$$

where $\mathbf D$ is the diagonal degree matrix. This operator is standard in graph signal processing (GSP) of neural data [@shuman_emerging_2013; @ortega_graph_2018]. Its eigendecomposition

$$
\mathcal L = \mathbf U \mathbf\Lambda \mathbf U^\top
$$

yields the graph harmonics, the columns $u_1, \ldots, u_N$ of $\mathbf U$, and their graph frequencies, the eigenvalues in $\mathbf\Lambda$, sorted in ascending order. Low-frequency harmonics vary smoothly across strongly connected dipoles, whereas high-frequency harmonics vary rapidly. The graph Fourier transform (GFT) expresses source activity $\mathbf x$ in this basis, $\hat{\mathbf x} = \mathbf U^\top \mathbf x$, and its entries are the graph Fourier coefficients on which CSET and wCSET place their priors. When the graph is a connectome, these graph harmonics are the connectome harmonics introduced earlier. For the geometric surrogate (GBF), the eigenvectors of the Laplace–Beltrami operator of the cortical mesh, known as geometric harmonics, replace the connectome harmonics in $\mathbf U$.

### Inverse Problem and Methods {#sec-inverse}

All three studies compare six methods: three minimum-norm baselines, wMNE [@hamalainen_interpreting_1994], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000] and sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002]; the connectome-based methods CSET and wCSET; and the geometry-based method GBF. Before reconstruction, the data and gain matrix were whitened with a noise covariance estimated from baseline epochs [@dale_dynamic_2000; @knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Study II provides only averaged responses, without baseline epochs, so we whitened its data and gain matrix with a diagonal noise covariance built from the sensor variances (@sec-data-resection).

**Common formulation.** All six methods estimate the source activity $\mathbf s \in \mathbb R^n$ from the EEG $\mathbf y \in \mathbb R^m$ and the gain matrix $\mathbf L$ (@sec-bem) by solving

$$
\mathbf s^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf s}\; \lVert \mathbf y - \mathbf L \mathbf s \rVert_2^2 + \alpha \lVert \mathbf C \mathbf s \rVert_p^p, \tag{1}
$$

where $\alpha$ balances data fit against the prior (@sec-lambda). The methods differ only in the prior, which is set by the matrix $\mathbf C$ and the norm $p$. For $p = 2$, the prior is Gaussian with source covariance $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} = (\mathbf C^\top \mathbf C)^{-1}$, and Eq. (1) has the closed-form solution

$$
\mathbf s^* = \mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}\mathbf L^\top\left(\mathbf L\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}\mathbf L^\top + \alpha\mathbf I\right)^{-1}\mathbf y, \tag{2}
$$

which we compute efficiently through a singular value decomposition, as in MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013] (@sec-annex-solvers). For $p = 1$, Eq. (1) has no closed form, and we solve it by proximal gradient descent. For every method, we normalize the prior covariance $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ to unit trace, so that $\alpha$ has the same scale across methods. For every method, we normalize the prior covariance $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$ to unit trace, so that $\alpha$ has the same scale across methods.

**Independent-source priors.** The three baselines use $p = 2$ with a diagonal $\mathbf C$. For dSPM and sLORETA it is the identity, and the solution is standardized afterward. For wMNE it is a depth-weighting matrix $\mathbf W_d^{-1}$, which counteracts the bias toward superficial dipoles (@sec-annex-baselines). Because $\mathbf C$ is diagonal, so is $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$. The sources are therefore independent a priori, and nothing in the prior encodes which regions co-activate.

**Connectome-based priors.** CSET and wCSET instead apply the prior to the graph Fourier coefficients of the depth-weighted activity, $\mathbf U^\top \mathbf W_d^{-1} \mathbf s$. The matrix $\mathbf C$ is then no longer diagonal, and the connectome harmonics couple the sources. CSET [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024] uses a sparse prior ($p = 1$), which favors activity represented by a few connectome harmonics, whatever their frequency. wCSET uses a Gaussian prior ($p = 2$) and adds harmonic weights that decay exponentially with graph frequency:

$$
\mathbf s^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf s}\; \lVert \mathbf y - \mathbf L \mathbf s \rVert_2^2 + \alpha \lVert \mathbf W_h^{-1} \mathbf U^\top \mathbf W_d^{-1} \mathbf s \rVert_2^2, \qquad W_{h,ii} = e^{-\beta \lambda_i}, \tag{3}
$$

where $\lambda_i \in [0, 2]$ is the graph frequency of harmonic $i$. The penalty grows with graph frequency, so the prior acts as an exponential low-pass filter on the connectome spectrum, with source covariance $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s} = \mathbf W_d \mathbf U \mathbf W_h^2 \mathbf U^\top \mathbf W_d$. We tuned $\beta = 5$ and, for both CSET and wCSET, the depth-weighting exponent ($\kappa = 0.2$, weaker than wMNE's $\kappa = 2$) in simulation (@sec-annex-tuning). Because its prior is Gaussian, wCSET, unlike CSET, has a closed-form solution: Eq. (2) with this covariance.

**Geometry-based prior.** GBF [@wang_geometry_2026] has the same form as wCSET, with three changes: geometric harmonics replace connectome harmonics (@sec-connectome), no depth weighting is applied, and $\mathbf W_h$ follows GBF's logarithmic decay, truncated after $S$ harmonics (@sec-annex-gbf). Because trace normalization cancels the effect of GBF's logarithmic parameter, we retuned the cutoff instead, with the same procedure as for wCSET, and obtained $S = 150$ rather than the published $S = 300$ (@sec-annex-gbf). GBF serves as the geometric surrogate in Study I (@sec-s1-surrogates) and as a comparison method in Studies II and III.

### Regularization Parameter Selection {#sec-lambda}

For all methods except CSET, we set the regularization parameter separately for each reconstruction from the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the evoked response, following MNE-Python's convention $\alpha = 1/\text{SNR}^2$. We estimated the SNR from the peak amplitude of the response and bounded the parameter below, $\alpha = \max(0.01,\, 1/\text{SNR}^2)$, so that regularization does not vanish at high SNR. CSET is the exception: because this convention applies to Gaussian ($p = 2$) priors, we fixed its parameter at $\alpha = 0.1$, tuned in simulation (@sec-annex-tuning).

## Datasets and Study-Specific Settings {#sec-datasets}

### Synthetic Data (Study I) {#sec-data-synthetic}

Study I simulates EEG from the anatomy of one subject of the VEPCON dataset [@pascucci_source_2022], which provides a T1-weighted MRI and a tractogram reconstructed from diffusion MRI (@sec-annex-vepcon). The EEG was simulated on the same 204-channel montage as in Studies II and III (@sec-data-resection), projected onto the subject's scalp surface (@sec-bem).

<!-- To put in annex: tractogram details -->

Each run starts from an initial patch of activity in one cortical region. We parcellated the source space (@sec-source-space) into 446 regions, using the cortical parcellation of the MultiConn atlas at scale 4 (@sec-connectome), and selected 100 of these regions by farthest-point sampling, so that the initial patches are spread evenly over the cortex. All Study I analyses use these 100 regions, except the noise-robustness analysis (@sec-s1-data-noise). That analysis simulates each region at several SNR levels, so it uses a smaller, independently sampled set of 50 regions.

**Source activity.** All dipoles of the initial patch receive the same 50 ms double-Hanning waveform, which mimics a clinical interictal spike [@dewouters_source-reconstructed_2026]. This follows approaches that model epileptiform activity as a patch of simultaneously active dipoles rather than a point source [@afnan_eegmeg_2024]. The spike repeats every second over a 20 s run, which gives 20 spikes per run and leaves time for the propagation from one spike to end before the next (@sec-annex-propagation).

<!-- To put in annex: The 1 s interval between spikes leaves time for propagation to end: no propagated activity was visible in the evoked baseline. Any residual activity would enter the noise covariance used for whitening, which all methods share, and so would not favor any of them. -->

**Propagation model.** From the initial patch, activity spreads outward through the individual connectome (@sec-connectome), without feedback: each dipole $j$ receives a delayed and attenuated copy of the source waveform $s_0$,

$$
s_j(t) = \gamma^{h_j}\, s_0(t - \tau_j),
$$

where $h_j$ is the number of connectome edges (hops) between the initial patch and dipole $j$, $\gamma = 0.5$ is the attenuation per hop, and $\tau_j$ is a delay that combines conduction speed, nodal delay and timing jitter (@sec-annex-propagation).

**Forward model.** Simulating and reconstructing with the same forward model, a practice known as the inverse crime, inflates reconstruction accuracy [@wirgin_inverse_2004]. We therefore projected the simulated activity to the sensors with a second forward solution, whose skull conductivity (0.012 S/m) is twice that used for reconstruction (0.006 S/m, @sec-bem). The two gain matrices differ by a relative difference measure (RDM) of about 10% (@sec-annex-forward).

**Noise model.** We added pink noise at the source level and white noise at the sensor level, scaled to a baseline of 15 µV RMS, typical of scalp EEG [@nunez_electric_2006], and to a single-spike SNR of 5, which the noise-robustness analysis varies (@sec-s1-data-noise; parameter values in @sec-annex-noise).

**Preprocessing and averaging.** Each run was re-referenced to the common average [@bertrand_theoretical_1985], cut into 20 epochs around the spikes and baseline-corrected. We estimated the noise covariance used for whitening (@sec-inverse) from the pre-spike period of the epochs, then averaged the epochs into one evoked response per run.

**Number of runs and regions.** We simulated 8 runs per region. A power analysis (@sec-annex-power) set the number of runs and of regions (100) so that the comparisons paired by region in the Results are adequately powered. The noise analysis repeats every simulation at each SNR level, so to keep the number of runs manageable, it used only 50 of the 100 regions. It therefore detects only larger differences than the main analysis.

**Connectome perturbation.** Because the simulated activity propagates through the individual connectome, and CSET and wCSET reconstruct with that same connectome, the simulation may favor them, a second form of inverse crime. The surrogate connectomes (@tbl-surrogates) and the added noise partly address this. A dedicated analysis quantifies it directly by perturbing the connectome used for reconstruction but not the one used for simulation (@sec-s1-prior-noise). Each perturbation swaps the endpoints of two randomly chosen edges, which preserves the degree of every dipole (a degree-preserving double-edge swap). Severity ranged from 0% to 100% of edges swapped.

### Epilepsy Surgery Data (Study II) {#sec-data-resection}

Study II uses the dataset of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025: 44 patients with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy who underwent resective surgery, each with a pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI and a pre-operative high-density interictal EEG. Surgical outcome was graded on the ILAE scale at 12 months (1 = seizure-free; 2–6 = increasingly poor outcomes). No diffusion MRI is available, so Study II uses the atlas surrogate connectome (@sec-connectome).

**Patient selection and reference.** The resection can serve as the reference only if it contained the epileptogenic zone, and seizure freedom after surgery confirms that it did. We therefore kept only the 28 seizure-free patients (ILAE 1). In patients with persistent seizures, the resection may have missed part of the epileptogenic zone. We excluded two more patients, one without a genuine resection cavity and one without the electrode positions needed for co-registration, which left 26 patients.

**EEG.** Clinical experts among the dataset's authors had identified interictal spikes visually and averaged them time-locked to their peak. The data providers had also filtered, downsampled and interpolated the recordings, and provided them in both a 257-channel (HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net) and a 204-channel version (@sec-annex-resection). We used the 204-channel version, which excludes the cheek electrodes, since these rarely capture brain activity. We then re-referenced the data to the common average and applied baseline correction, and we removed residual line noise with a 50 Hz notch filter for recordings whose power spectrum showed a 50 Hz peak. Because only averaged spikes were available, we could not estimate a noise covariance from baseline epochs, and we whitened the data with a diagonal covariance built from the sensor variances (@sec-inverse).

**Resection masks.** We segmented each resection with RAMPS [@simpson_automated_2025], which estimates the resected volume from the pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI. RAMPS requires the hemisphere and lobe of the resection as input, which we identified visually on the post-operative MRI. We checked every mask visually by overlaying it on both MRIs. The automated masks were satisfactory for 20 patients, and we segmented the remaining 6 manually (@sec-annex-resection).

### Simultaneous EEG–iEEG Data (Study III) {#sec-data-ieeg}

Study III uses a cohort of four patients with epilepsy, recorded with the protocol of @roehri_scalp-negative_2025. Each patient was recorded simultaneously with scalp EEG, on the same 204-channel montage as Studies I and II, and with intracranial EEG (iEEG) from depth electrodes. Interictal spikes were detected on the iEEG with the automated detector Delphos [@roehri_time-frequency_2016; @roehri_assets_2017]. Both modalities were then epoched around the same spikes, which gives paired scalp and intracranial recordings of the same activity (130–265 spikes per patient). Each patient's T1-weighted MRI was processed with the same pipeline as in the other studies (@sec-pipeline). As in Study II, no diffusion MRI is available, so Study III uses the atlas surrogate connectome (@sec-connectome).

**EEG.** The EEG epochs were preprocessed as in Study I, with re-referencing to the common average, baseline correction and estimation of the noise covariance from the pre-spike period. They were then averaged into one evoked response per patient.

**Reference: recorded and virtual iEEG.** The iEEG epochs were averaged, without further preprocessing, into the reference evoked response. Because iEEG samples the potential only at a sparse set of contacts, we compared each reconstruction with the recorded iEEG at those contacts only, following @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026. For this comparison, we projected each reconstruction onto the contacts, which gives a virtual iEEG. We calculated the potential that each reconstructed dipole produces at each contact, assuming an infinite homogeneous conductor, and summed these potentials over dipoles. Where a dipole lay closer than 3 mm to a contact, the assumed accuracy of the iEEG–MRI co-registration, we set the distance to 3 mm, which prevents the potential from growing without bound near the source.

**Comparison window.** @grova_intracranial_2016 compared virtual and recorded iEEG over a few samples around the spike peak, which mainly captures the onset of activity. Because we expect connectivity-informed methods to improve the reconstruction mostly after onset, we compared the two signals over a longer window. For each patient, this window covers the samples where the global field power (GFP) of the recorded iEEG exceeds a threshold set from its baseline, so that the data define the window (@sec-annex-ieeg).

**Patients reported.** The main text reports two of the four patients. In the other two, the spikes originate from deep sources, far from the cortical source space (@sec-source-space). Because the reconstruction cannot place activity there, the virtual iEEG at the contacts near these sources is unreliable, so their results appear in the Annex. With two patients in the main analysis, Study III serves as a proof of concept rather than a statistical validation.

## Evaluation Metrics {#sec-metrics}

Each study compares the reconstructions with its ground truth or reference using one or two of three metrics (@tbl-metrics).

| Metric | Study I (simulations) | Study II (epilepsy surgery) | Study III (simultaneous EEG–iEEG) |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Localization error | 25% of the rising phase | 50% of the rising phase | — |
| Spatial correlation | Pearson, across dipoles, over time | — | Pearson, across contacts, averaged over the comparison window |
| Spatial overlap (AUC) | — | — | Annex only |

: Metrics used in each study. {#tbl-metrics}

### Localization Error {#sec-metric-loc}

The localization error is the Euclidean distance from the dipole with the largest absolute reconstructed amplitude to the boundary of the target region, which is the initial patch in Study I and the resection volume in Study II. The error is 0 mm if this dipole lies inside the target region [@wang_geometry_2026].

We measured it during the rising phase of the spike rather than at its peak, by which time activity has usually spread. Early in the rising phase, activity is still focal but the SNR is low. Later, the SNR is higher but activity has begun to spread. In Study I, we used the time point at which the spike reaches 25% of its peak amplitude, when the simulated activity is still confined to the initial patch. In Study II, we used the time point at which it reaches 50%, which @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020 found most accurate on this dataset.

### Spatial Correlation {#sec-metric-corr}

At each time point, the spatial correlation measures how well the pattern of reconstructed activity matches the ground truth or reference. In Study I, it is the Pearson correlation, across dipoles, between the reconstructed and simulated activity. In Study III, it is the Pearson correlation, across intracranial contacts, between the virtual and recorded iEEG (@sec-data-ieeg). Previous studies comparing source reconstructions with simultaneous intracranial recordings used the same measure [@grova_intracranial_2016; @afnan_assessing_2026]. Like any correlation, it ignores the different amplitude scales of the two signals.

@grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026 evaluated this correlation at the spike peak. Because co-activation develops over the course of the spike, not only at its peak, we instead averaged the correlation over the comparison window, which covers all time points at which the activity rises above the noise (@sec-data-ieeg). For direct comparison with their results, the Annex also reports the correlation at the peak, averaged over five samples as in @grova_intracranial_2016, and the AUC used by @afnan_assessing_2026 (@sec-metric-auc).

### Area Under the ROC Curve {#sec-metric-auc}

For direct comparison with @afnan_assessing_2026, the Annex also reports the area under the ROC curve (AUC), a measure of spatial overlap [@grova_evaluation_2006]. At the spike peak, contacts whose recorded absolute amplitude reached at least 30% of the maximum were labeled active, as in @afnan_assessing_2026. The AUC is the probability that the virtual iEEG has a larger absolute amplitude at an active contact than at an inactive one. It equals 0.5 at chance and 1 for perfect separation.

## Statistical Analysis {#sec-stats}

### Method Comparisons {#sec-stats-tests}

All method comparisons are paired, and each method is compared with wCSET. We report every effect in the units of its outcome (millimeters of localization error, difference in correlation Δr, or difference in the proportion of patients), with its 95% confidence interval (CI), so that its size can be judged directly. p-values were corrected with the Holm procedure [@holm_simple_1979] within each family of comparisons, formed by one outcome in one study (or one patient in Study III) across the methods compared with wCSET (α = 0.05).

**Studies I and II.** Outcomes with one value per pair were compared with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test [@wilcoxon_individual_1945], keeping zero differences [@pratt_remarks_1959]. Pairs are regions in Study I, each the mean over its eight runs, and patients in Study II. As the effect size, we report the Hodges–Lehmann estimate of the paired difference with its distribution-free CI [@hodges_estimates_1963]. The figures also give the rank-biserial correlation [@kerby_simple_2014]. Whether the peak fell inside the resection volume (Study II) is binary, so we compared it with the exact McNemar test [@mcnemar_note_1947] and report the difference in the proportion of patients, with Newcombe's CI [@newcombe_improved_1998]. Outcomes that vary along a continuous dimension (time, SNR or perturbation severity) were compared with cluster-based permutation tests on the paired differences [@maris_nonparametric_2007], with 3,000 permutations and Holm correction across methods applied to each method's most significant cluster. For each significant cluster, we report the paired difference averaged over its extent, with the same effect size as above: the Hodges–Lehmann estimate for localization error and the mean, with a t-based CI, for spatial correlation.

**Non-inferiority.** A method was considered non-inferior to its comparator when the 95% CI of the reported effect ruled out being worse by more than a margin δ. For localization error, δ = 5 mm, the error that the head model alone introduces in EEG source localization [@akalin_acar_effects_2013]. For spatial correlation, δ = 0.1, which corresponds to Cohen's smallest effect for a difference between two correlations (q = 0.1) at the correlation levels observed here [@cohen_statistical_1988]. These margins apply to wCSET against the other methods and to the surrogate connectomes against the individual connectome (@sec-s1-surrogates).

**Study III.** In each patient, the outcome is computed on a single averaged spike, so its uncertainty depends on which spikes enter that average. The time points within the average cannot serve as independent samples, because successive time points are strongly correlated. We therefore analyzed each patient separately with a paired bootstrap over spikes [@field_bootstrapping_2007; @cameron_bootstrap-based_2008]. In each of 1,000 draws, we resampled the spikes with replacement, averaged them, and recomputed every method's virtual iEEG and its spatial correlation with the recorded iEEG over the comparison window. Spikes close enough in time to share samples were resampled together. The draws give the 95% CI of the difference between wCSET and each method, and the corresponding p-value (@sec-annex-bootstrap).

### Chance Level {#sec-metric-chance}

For the spatial correlation of Study III, we estimated chance levels as in @afnan_assessing_2026. We randomly permuted the contact labels of the virtual iEEG 1,000 times, recomputed the correlation at every time point, and took the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting null distribution.

## Study I: Simulations {#sec-study1}

### Localization vs. Co-Activation {#sec-s1-localization}

We tested both parts of our hypothesis (@sec-introduction) on the simulation described in @sec-data-synthetic, in which activity spreads from a single known source and the ground truth is fully known (@fig-flagship-example).

At 25% of the peak amplitude (@sec-metric-loc), wCSET's localization error was significantly lower than sLORETA's and wMNE's, but significantly higher than CSET's and dSPM's (@fig-s1-localization a; all p_corrected < 0.001). By the Hodges–Lehmann estimate, it was lower than sLORETA's by 8.6 mm (95% CI 5.3 to 11.6) and wMNE's by 45.2 mm (95% CI 41.0 to 49.3), but higher than CSET's by 5.2 mm (95% CI 2.3 to 7.8) and dSPM's by 6.2 mm (95% CI 2.8 to 9.4). The upper bounds of both deficits (7.8 and 9.4 mm) exceed 5 mm, the localization error that the head model alone introduces [@akalin_acar_effects_2013], so wCSET was not shown to localize the onset as well as CSET and dSPM at this SNR. wCSET's errors were bimodal. It placed its peak inside the initial patch in 27% of regions, more often than any other method (CSET 24%, dSPM 9%), but more than 30 mm away from it in 24% (CSET 13%, dSPM 4%). @sec-s1-data-noise shows how this pattern changes with SNR.

In spatial correlation, wCSET outperformed every other method throughout the spike, from onset (0 ms) until 80–88 ms depending on the method (@fig-s1-localization b; all p_corrected ≤ 0.001). Its advantage was larger over the standard methods than over CSET, and it grew as activity spread from the initial patch. As mean paired differences across regions, wCSET's correlation exceeded the standard methods' by Δr = 0.16–0.17 (all lower CI bounds ≥ `{python} corr1_std_ci_lo_25`) and CSET's by Δr = 0.07 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.09) at 25% of the peak amplitude. At the peak, these differences reached Δr = 0.28–0.29 (all lower CI bounds ≥ `{python} corr1_std_ci_lo_pp`) and 0.10 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.12). The gap between connectivity-informed and standard methods was largest at 16 ms, close to the peak. Before onset and after the spike, the averaged EEG contains only noise, so all correlations stay near zero there and are not interpreted.

```{python filename="simf_localization_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

DELTA_LOC_MM = 5.0  # non-inferiority margin: the head model's own localization error floor [@akalin_acar_effects_2013]

simf_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/flagship")
competitors = [m for m in METHODS if m != "wcset"]
comparisons = simf_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors)

# Localization error at qrp: Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. wCSET, paired by region (mean over its repetitions),
# ties kept (Pratt), Holm across the 4 competitors. Hodges-Lehmann shift (mm) and rank-biserial r, each
# with its 95% CI.
loc1_results = simf_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
    "localization_error", group_by="Method", comparisons=comparisons, pairing_col="region",
    filters={"phase": "qrp"}, correction="holm", zero_method="pratt",
    effect_sizes=("hodges_lehmann", "rank_biserial"), ci_seed=0,
)
_loc1 = loc1_results.vs("wcset", higher_is_better=False)  # positive = wCSET better (lower error)

# Non-inferiority: wCSET's error exceeds the competitor's by less than DELTA_LOC_MM, i.e. the whole
# Hodges-Lehmann CI lies above -DELTA_LOC_MM.
loc1_noninferior = (_loc1["hodges_lehmann_ci_low"] > -DELTA_LOC_MM).to_dict()

# Statistics quoted in the prose. The prose says wCSET beats sLORETA and wMNE, trails CSET and dSPM, and
# is not shown non-inferior to either: checked here.
assert (_loc1.loc[["sloreta", "wmne"], "hodges_lehmann"] > 0).all() and (_loc1.loc[["cset", "dspm"], "hodges_lehmann"] < 0).all()
assert _loc1["significant"].all() and not loc1_noninferior["cset"] and not loc1_noninferior["dspm"]

def _flip(row, name):
    """`row`'s `name` estimate and CI with the sign reversed, to quote a deficit as a positive number."""
    return {name: -row[name], f"{name}_ci_low": -row[f"{name}_ci_high"], f"{name}_ci_high": -row[f"{name}_ci_low"]}

loc1_p_max = fmt_p(_loc1["p_corrected"].max())
loc1_sloreta_hl, loc1_wmne_hl = (fmt_ci(_loc1.loc[c], "hodges_lehmann", unit=" mm") for c in ["sloreta", "wmne"])
loc1_cset_hl, loc1_dspm_hl = (fmt_ci(_flip(_loc1.loc[c], "hodges_lehmann"), "hodges_lehmann", unit=" mm") for c in ["cset", "dspm"])
loc1_small_r = fmt_num(_loc1.loc[["cset", "dspm"], "rank_biserial"].abs().mean(), 1)  # size of wCSET's deficits (Discussion)
loc1_delta = fmt_num(DELTA_LOC_MM, 0)
loc1_cset_hi, loc1_dspm_hi = (fmt_num(-_loc1.loc[c, "hodges_lehmann_ci_low"]) for c in ["cset", "dspm"])  # upper CI bounds of the deficits
_loc_trials = simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp"})
simf_n_regions = _loc_trials["region"].nunique()
simf_loc_trial_median_wcset = fmt_num(_loc_trials.loc[_loc_trials["Method"] == "wcset", "Value"].median())  # over all trials

# Bimodal errors, over all simulations: share with the peak inside the initial patch (0 mm) and share more
# than 30 mm away. The prose says wCSET hits the patch most often.
_exact = _loc_trials.groupby("Method")["Value"].apply(lambda v: (v == 0).mean() * 100)
_far = _loc_trials.groupby("Method")["Value"].apply(lambda v: (v > 30).mean() * 100)
assert _exact.idxmax() == "wcset"
loc1_exact = {m: fmt_num(_exact[m], 0) for m in METHODS}
loc1_far = {m: fmt_num(_far[m], 0) for m in METHODS}
loc1_exact_wcset, loc1_exact_cset, loc1_exact_dspm = (loc1_exact[m] for m in ["wcset", "cset", "dspm"])
loc1_far_wcset, loc1_far_cset, loc1_far_dspm = (loc1_far[m] for m in ["wcset", "cset", "dspm"])

# Spatial correlation over time: cluster permutation vs. wCSET, paired by region; Holm across the 4 pairs,
# each on its smallest cluster p (family="pair"). Cached: reloaded unless the call or the data changed.
times_order = sorted(simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation")["times"].unique())
corr1_results = cached(
    simf_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation, "./results/simf/flagship/stats/corr_time_cluster",
    "correlation", coord="times", group_by="Method", comparisons=comparisons, pairing_col="region",
    coord_order=times_order, higher_is_better=True, correction="holm", family="pair",
    n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
)

# Statistics quoted in the prose: the largest cluster where wCSET is better (sign = +1), which spans
# the simulated spike. Clusters of the opposite sign fall in the baseline and after the spike, where
# the averaged EEG is noise only and the correlations are not interpretable.
def _better(competitor):
    clusters = corr1_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", competitor)]
    return main_cluster(clusters[clusters["sign"] == 1])

corr1_sloreta, corr1_dspm, corr1_wmne, corr1_cset = (_better(c) for c in ["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne", "cset"])
_better_clusters = [corr1_sloreta, corr1_dspm, corr1_wmne, corr1_cset]
# Quoted as "≤": with 3000 permutations, about 0.001 is the smallest p the test can return.
corr1_p_max = f"≤ {max(c['p_corrected'] for c in _better_clusters):.3f}"

# Approximate extent of the wCSET-better clusters (a cluster test does not establish exact onsets/offsets).
corr1_window_start = fmt_num(round(min(c["times_start"] for c in _better_clusters) * 1000), digits=0)
corr1_window_end_lo = fmt_num(min(c["times_end"] for c in _better_clusters) * 1000, digits=0)
corr1_window_end_hi = fmt_num(max(c["times_end"] for c in _better_clusters) * 1000, digits=0)

# Effect size: mean paired difference in correlation (wCSET - competitor, t 95% CI, like the t-based
# cluster test) at the median qrp and peak times, which fall on the 4 ms time grid.
qrp_median = float(simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="qrp_time")["Value"].median())
pp_median = float(simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="pp_time")["Value"].median())
_grid = np.asarray(times_order)

def _on_grid(t):
    tg = _grid[np.argmin(np.abs(_grid - t))]
    assert abs(tg - t) < 1e-4  # on the grid, so no interpolation is needed
    return tg

phase_times = {"qrp": _on_grid(qrp_median), "pp": _on_grid(pp_median)}
corr1_at = {
    phase: simf_metrics.estimate.mean_diff(
        "correlation", group_by="Method", comparisons=comparisons, pairing_col="region", filters={"times": t},
    ).vs("wcset")
    for phase, t in phase_times.items()
}
corr1_dr = {phase: {c: fmt_ci(est.loc[c], "estimate", digits=2) for c in competitors} for phase, est in corr1_at.items()}
_std = ["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]
corr1_std_dr_qrp_lo, corr1_std_dr_qrp_hi, corr1_std_dr_pp_lo, corr1_std_dr_pp_hi = (
    fmt_num(f(corr1_at[phase].loc[_std, "estimate"]), 2) for phase in ["qrp", "pp"] for f in [min, max])
corr1_cset_dr_qrp, corr1_cset_dr_pp = corr1_dr["qrp"]["cset"], corr1_dr["pp"]["cset"]

# Per-region curves (mean over repetitions), summarized across regions for panel b1, and the time of the
# largest gap between connectivity-informed and standard methods.
corr_collapsed = simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation").groupby(
    ["Method", "region", "times"], as_index=False,
)["Value"].mean()
corr_median_curve = corr_collapsed.groupby(["Method", "times"], as_index=False)["Value"].median()
corr_pivot = corr_median_curve.pivot(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").sort_index()
corr_gap = corr_pivot[["wcset", "cset"]].mean(axis=1) - corr_pivot[["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]].mean(axis=1)
corr1_gap_peak_time = fmt_num(corr_gap.idxmax() * 1000, digits=0)
```

```{python filename="simf_localization_correlation_plot.py"}
# Non-inferiority margin: wCSET worse by DELTA_LOC_MM
loc1_dax.axhline(-DELTA_LOC_MM, color="#0b0b0b", linestyle="--", linewidth=1, alpha=0.6, zorder=0.5)
loc1_dax.text(loc1_dax.get_xlim()[1], -DELTA_LOC_MM, f" −δ ({DELTA_LOC_MM:g} mm)", fontsize=8,
              ha="left", va="center", alpha=0.7)
loc1_dax.set_ylabel("Method − wCSET (mm)")
loc1_dax.set_title("a2. Localization error: paired difference vs. wCSET\n(per region)", loc="left", fontsize=10)

# (a) Median across regions (each region = mean over its runs) with IQR band; wCSET on top and first in the legend
simf_metrics.plot.line(
    "correlation", "times", hue="Method", unit="region", hue_order=["wcset"] + competitors, center="median",
    interval="iqr", highlight="wcset", palette=COLORS, fill_alpha=0.15, ax=corr1_ax,
    labels={**METHOD_LABELS, "wcset": f"{METHOD_LABELS['wcset']} (ref.)"},
    line_kws={m: {"color": matte(COLORS[m]), **({} if m == "wcset" else {"linewidth": 1.6})}
              for m in competitors + ["wcset"]},
)
corr1_ax.legend(*corr1_ax.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="upper right", fontsize=8, frameon=False)

# qrp and peak reference lines
corr1_ax.axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", linewidth=1, zorder=0)
corr1_ax.axvline(qrp_median, color="#0b0b0b", linestyle="--", linewidth=1, alpha=0.6, zorder=0.5)
corr1_ax.axvline(pp_median, color="#0b0b0b", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.2, alpha=0.6, zorder=0.5)
ymax = corr1_ax.get_ylim()[1]
corr1_ax.text(qrp_median, ymax, f" qrp (median, t={round(qrp_median*1000):.0f} ms)",
        fontsize=8, ha="left", va="top", rotation=90, alpha=0.7)
corr1_ax.text(pp_median, ymax, f" pp (median, t={round(pp_median*1000):.0f} ms)",
        fontsize=8, ha="left", va="top", rotation=90, alpha=0.7)

corr1_ax.set_xlabel("")
corr1_ax.set_ylabel("Spatial correlation\n(ground truth vs. reconstruction)")
corr1_ax.set_title("b1. Spatial correlation per method over time", loc="left", fontsize=10)
corr1_ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# (b) Paired differences over time: mean across regions with its pointwise t 95% CI (the cluster test is
# t-based). mindmap's own cluster bars are hidden: the rows below separate wCSET-better from wCSET-worse clusters.
simf_metrics.plot.paired_differences(
    corr1_results, reference="wcset", order=competitors, palette=COLORS, ax=corr1_dax,
    cluster_kws={"visible": False}, legend=False,
)
t = np.asarray(times_order)
_corr1_diff = simf_metrics.stat.paired_differences(corr1_results, reference="wcset")
_label_y = _corr1_diff[_corr1_diff["times"] == t[-1]].groupby("Method")["Value"].mean().to_dict()
_label_t = t[-1]

# Significant clusters, one row per competitor (colored: wCSET better, gray: worse)
_dy = np.ptp(corr1_dax.get_ylim())
_row_h = 0.035 * _dy
_row0 = corr1_dax.get_ylim()[0] - 0.02 * _dy
_step = (t[1] - t[0]) / 2
for k, c in enumerate(competitors):
    y = _row0 - (k + 1) * 1.4 * _row_h
    cl = corr1_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", c)]
    for _, row in cl[cl["significant"].astype(bool)].iterrows():
        better = row["sign"] > 0
        corr1_dax.fill_between([row["times_start"] - _step, row["times_end"] + _step], y, y + _row_h,
                               color=matte(COLORS[c]) if better else "#c3c2b7", linewidth=0, zorder=2)
    corr1_dax.text(t[0] - 3 * _step, y + _row_h / 2, METHOD_LABELS[c], fontsize=7,
                   ha="right", va="center", color="#444444")
_yticks = [v for v in corr1_dax.get_yticks() if _row0 <= v <= corr1_dax.get_ylim()[1]]
corr1_dax.set_ylim(_row0 - (len(competitors) + 0.6) * 1.4 * _row_h, corr1_dax.get_ylim()[1])
corr1_dax.set_yticks(_yticks)

# Direct labels at the line ends, spread apart to avoid overlap
_min_gap = 0.035 * np.ptp(corr1_dax.get_ylim())
_placed = []
for c in sorted(_label_y, key=_label_y.get):
    y = _label_y[c]
    if _placed and y - _placed[-1] < _min_gap:
        y = _placed[-1] + _min_gap
    _placed.append(y)
    corr1_dax.text(_label_t, y, f" {METHOD_LABELS[c]}", color="#222222", fontsize=8, va="center", ha="left")

corr1_dax.axvline(qrp_median, color="#0b0b0b", linestyle="--", linewidth=1, alpha=0.6, zorder=0.5)
corr1_dax.axvline(pp_median, color="#0b0b0b", linestyle=":", linewidth=1.2, alpha=0.6, zorder=0.5)
corr1_dax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
corr1_dax.set_ylabel("wCSET − method\n(spatial correlation)")
corr1_dax.set_title("b2. Spatial correlation: paired difference vs. wCSET (mean across regions, 95% CI)", loc="left", fontsize=10)
corr1_dax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# Column headers: each column is one metric, absolute values on top, paired differences below
column_headers(s1_fig, [(loc1_ax, "LOCALIZATION ERROR (quarter rising phase)"),
                        (corr1_ax, "SPATIAL CORRELATION (over time)")], y=0.955)
```

### Robustness to Data Noise {#sec-s1-data-noise}

We swept the single-spike SNR from 20 down to 1 (@sec-data-synthetic).

Localization error rose for every method as the SNR decreased (@fig-annex-noise-loc). wMNE degraded first, while the other four methods stayed accurate down to roughly SNR 3–5. wCSET was more accurate than wMNE across the whole range and never differed significantly from CSET. Against the other two standard methods, its advantage depended on the SNR. It was more accurate than sLORETA down to SNR 14 (p_corrected = 0.046) and than dSPM down to SNR 10 (p_corrected = 0.012). By the Hodges–Lehmann estimate, its error was lower than wMNE's by 25.0 mm (95% CI 22.1 to 27.9; p_corrected ≤ 0.001), and lower than sLORETA's and dSPM's by 3.3 mm (95% CI 1.6 to 5.2) and 6.2 mm (95% CI 3.3 to 9.1) over their clusters. Between SNR 10 and 5, wCSET's median error rose from 3.5 to 16.8 mm, while dSPM's stayed at 11.6–12.3 mm. At SNR 3, the difference reversed in dSPM's favor, though not significantly (p_corrected = 0.085). The SNR of the main simulation (5) thus lies where wCSET loses its advantage over dSPM, consistent with its deficit in @sec-s1-localization.

Spatial correlation was more robust. wCSET's advantage held down to SNR 3 against the standard methods and down to SNR 2 against CSET, both at 25% of the peak amplitude and at the peak (@fig-annex-noise-corr; all p_corrected ≤ 0.001). As mean paired differences over each cluster, wCSET's correlation exceeded the other methods' by Δr = 0.12–0.42. Below these SNRs, the spike could no longer be distinguished from the noise. Every method's correlation fell close to zero, and wCSET's was slightly lower (all p_corrected ≤ 0.038).

```{python filename="simf_noise_summary_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# Same tests as the Annex (cached, shared): cluster permutation over SNR, wCSET vs. each competitor,
# region-paired, Holm across the 4 pairs (family="pair"). sign = +1 = wCSET better.
noise_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/noise_sweep")
competitors = [m for m in METHODS if m != "wcset"]
standard = ["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]

def _snr_order(metric):
    return sorted(noise_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": "qrp"})["snr"].unique(), reverse=True)

def _noise_test(metric, phase, higher_is_better):
    return cached(
        noise_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation, f"./results/simf/noise_sweep/stats/{metric}_{phase}_cluster",
        metric, coord="snr", group_by="Method",
        comparisons=noise_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
        coord_order=_snr_order(metric), higher_is_better=higher_is_better, filters={"phase": phase},
        correction="holm", family="pair", n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
    )

def _cluster(clusters, sign):
    """Largest cluster of the given sign, or None if there is none."""
    rows = clusters[clusters["sign"] == sign] if not clusters.empty else clusters
    return None if rows.empty else main_cluster(rows)

noise_loc = _noise_test("localization_error", "qrp", higher_is_better=False)
noise_corr = {phase: _noise_test("correlation", phase, higher_is_better=True) for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]}

def _cluster_diff(metric, phase, competitor, cluster, higher_is_better):
    """Paired difference over a cluster's SNR span (one value per region, averaged over the span and the
    repetitions), oriented so that positive = wCSET better, with its 95% CI: the Hodges-Lehmann estimate for
    localization error and the mean for correlation, as in @sec-s1-localization."""
    snrs = [s for s in _snr_order(metric) if cluster["snr_end"] <= s <= cluster["snr_start"]]
    estimator = noise_metrics.estimate.hodges_lehmann if metric == "localization_error" else noise_metrics.estimate.mean_diff
    return estimator(
        metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=[("wcset", competitor)], pairing_col="region",
        filters={"phase": phase, "snr": snrs},
    ).vs("wcset", higher_is_better=higher_is_better).loc[competitor]

# Localization error: wCSET-better clusters per competitor (CSET: no cluster at all), and against dSPM a
# non-significant wCSET-worse cluster at low SNR.
_loc = {c: _cluster(noise_loc.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", c)], 1) for c in competitors}
assert _loc["cset"] is None
_loc_d = {c: _cluster_diff("localization_error", "qrp", c, _loc[c], False) for c in ["wmne", "dspm", "sloreta"]}
noise_loc_wmne_d, noise_loc_wmne_p = fmt_ci(_loc_d["wmne"], "estimate", unit=" mm"), f"≤ {_loc['wmne']['p_corrected']:.3f}"  # "≤": ~0.001 is the smallest p of 3000 permutations
noise_loc_dspm_end, noise_loc_sloreta_end = fmt_num(_loc["dspm"]["snr_end"], 0), fmt_num(_loc["sloreta"]["snr_end"], 0)
noise_loc_dspm_d, noise_loc_sloreta_d = (fmt_ci(_loc_d[c], "estimate", unit=" mm") for c in ["dspm", "sloreta"])
noise_loc_dspm_p, noise_loc_sloreta_p = fmt_p(_loc["dspm"]["p_corrected"]), fmt_p(_loc["sloreta"]["p_corrected"])
_dspm_worse = _cluster(noise_loc.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", "dspm")], -1)
assert _dspm_worse is not None and not _dspm_worse["significant"] and _dspm_worse["snr_start"] == _dspm_worse["snr_end"]
noise_loc_dspm_worse_snr, noise_loc_dspm_worse_p = fmt_num(_dspm_worse["snr_start"], 0), fmt_p(_dspm_worse["p_corrected"])

# Median localization error per SNR (one value per region, the mean over its repetitions): wCSET's rises
# sharply between SNR 10 and 5, dSPM's stays flat down to SNR 5.
_loc_med = (noise_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp"})
            .groupby(["Method", "snr", "region"])["Value"].mean().groupby(["Method", "snr"]).median())
noise_loc_wcset_med_10, noise_loc_wcset_med_5 = fmt_num(_loc_med["wcset", 10]), fmt_num(_loc_med["wcset", 5])
noise_loc_dspm_med_lo = fmt_num(_loc_med["dspm"].loc[5:].min())
noise_loc_dspm_med_hi = fmt_num(_loc_med["dspm"].loc[5:].max())

# Spatial correlation, both phases: wCSET-better clusters down to some SNR, wCSET-worse clusters below it.
_better = {(ph, c): _cluster(noise_corr[ph].clusters_by_pair[("wcset", c)], 1) for ph in noise_corr for c in competitors}
_worse = {(ph, c): _cluster(noise_corr[ph].clusters_by_pair[("wcset", c)], -1) for ph in noise_corr for c in competitors}
noise_corr_end_std = fmt_num(max(_better[(ph, c)]["snr_end"] for ph in noise_corr for c in standard), 0)
noise_corr_end_cset = fmt_num(max(_better[(ph, "cset")]["snr_end"] for ph in noise_corr), 0)
_better_d = [_cluster_diff("correlation", ph, c, b, True)["estimate"] for (ph, c), b in _better.items()]
noise_corr_d_lo, noise_corr_d_hi = fmt_num(min(_better_d), 2), fmt_num(max(_better_d), 2)
noise_corr_p_max = f"≤ {max(b['p_corrected'] for b in _better.values()):.3f}"  # "≤": ~0.001 is the smallest p of 3000 permutations
noise_corr_worse_p_max = f'{max(w["p_corrected"] for w in _worse.values() if w is not None):.3f}'
```


### Robustness to Prior Noise {#sec-s1-prior-noise}

```{python filename="simf_degradation_summary_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

deg_metrics_summary = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/degradation")

# Medians per method and perturbation level. sLORETA and dSPM are connectome-agnostic: their flagship values
# are repeated at every level (processing_simf.qmd, Suite Assembly), so their median at 0% is their reference.
def _deg_medians(metric):
    df = deg_metrics_summary.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": "qrp"})
    return df.groupby(["Method", "percentage"])["Value"].median().unstack("percentage")

_loc_med_summary = _deg_medians("localization_error")
_corr_med_summary = _deg_medians("correlation")

# localization error (mm): wCSET's gradual rise vs. CSET's flat-then-sharp pattern
deg_summary_ref_loc_sloreta = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["sloreta", 0])
deg_summary_ref_loc_dspm = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["dspm", 0])
deg_summary_loc_wcset_0 = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["wcset", 0])
deg_summary_loc_wcset_100 = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["wcset", 100])
deg_summary_loc_cset_lo_s = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 0:60].min())
deg_summary_loc_cset_hi_s = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 0:60].max())
deg_summary_loc_cset_100 = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 100])

# spatial correlation: wCSET's gradual decline vs. CSET's flat-then-sharp pattern
deg_summary_ref_corr_sloreta = fmt_num(_corr_med_summary.loc["sloreta", 0], 2)
deg_summary_ref_corr_dspm = fmt_num(_corr_med_summary.loc["dspm", 0], 2)
deg_summary_corr_wcset_0 = fmt_num(_corr_med_summary.loc["wcset", 0], 2)
deg_summary_corr_wcset_100 = fmt_num(_corr_med_summary.loc["wcset", 100], 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_lo_s = fmt_num(_corr_med_summary.loc["cset", 0:60].min(), 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_hi_s = fmt_num(_corr_med_summary.loc["cset", 0:60].max(), 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_100 = fmt_num(_corr_med_summary.loc["cset", 100], 2)

# Same tests as the Annex (cached, shared): cluster permutation over perturbation level, CSET/wCSET vs. each
# connectome-agnostic reference (sLORETA, dSPM), region-paired, Holm across the 4 pairs (family="pair"). The
# reference comes first in each pair, so sign = -1 means CSET/wCSET is better.
DEG_REFERENCES = ["sloreta", "dspm"]
def _deg_test(metric, higher_is_better):
    order = sorted(deg_metrics_summary.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": "qrp"})["percentage"].unique())
    return cached(
        deg_metrics_summary.stat.cluster_permutation, f"./results/simf/degradation/stats/{metric}_qrp_cluster",
        metric, coord="percentage", group_by="Method",
        comparisons=deg_metrics_summary.stat.build_comparisons(DEG_REFERENCES, ["cset", "wcset"]),
        pairing_col="region", coord_order=order, higher_is_better=higher_is_better, filters={"phase": "qrp"},
        correction="holm", family="pair", n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
    )

_DEG_METRICS = {"loc": ("localization_error", False), "corr": ("correlation", True)}
_deg = {m: _deg_test(metric, higher_is_better=hib) for m, (metric, hib) in _DEG_METRICS.items()}

def _deg_cluster(metric, ref, method, better):
    clusters = _deg[metric].clusters_by_pair[(ref, method)]
    rows = clusters[clusters["sign"] == (-1 if better else 1)]
    return None if rows.empty else main_cluster(rows)

def _deg_diff(metric, ref, method, cluster):
    """Paired difference vs. `ref` over the cluster's perturbation span, positive = `method` better: the
    Hodges-Lehmann estimate for localization error and the mean for correlation, as in @sec-s1-localization."""
    name, hib = _DEG_METRICS[metric]
    levels = [p for p in deg_metrics_summary.to_df(metrics=name, filters={"phase": "qrp"})["percentage"].unique()
              if cluster["percentage_start"] <= p <= cluster["percentage_end"]]
    estimator = deg_metrics_summary.estimate.hodges_lehmann if metric == "loc" else deg_metrics_summary.estimate.mean_diff
    est = estimator(
        name, group_by="Method", comparisons=[(ref, method)], pairing_col="region",
        filters={"phase": "qrp", "percentage": levels},
    ).vs(method, higher_is_better=hib).loc[ref]
    digits, unit = (1, " mm") if metric == "loc" else (2, "")
    return (f"{est['estimate']:+.{digits}f}{unit}, 95% CI {est['ci_low']:.{digits}f} to {est['ci_high']:.{digits}f}")

# deg_<metric>_<method>_<ref>_{better,worse}_*: the largest cluster where `method` beats `ref` (or loses to it),
# its span, effect and p_corrected.
for _m in ["loc", "corr"]:
    for _ref in DEG_REFERENCES:
        for _method in ["cset", "wcset"]:
            for _kind, _c in [("better", _deg_cluster(_m, _ref, _method, True)), ("worse", _deg_cluster(_m, _ref, _method, False))]:
                if _c is None:
                    continue
                _key = f"deg_{_m}_{_method}_{_ref}_{_kind}"
                globals()[f"{_key}_start"] = fmt_num(_c["percentage_start"], 0)
                globals()[f"{_key}_end"] = fmt_num(_c["percentage_end"], 0)
                globals()[f"{_key}_d"] = _deg_diff(_m, _ref, _method, _c)
                globals()[f"{_key}_p"] = fmt_p(_c["p_corrected"])
```

We perturbed an increasing share of the connectome's edges (@sec-data-synthetic) and compared CSET and wCSET with the connectome-agnostic sLORETA at the quarter rising phase (differences averaged over each cluster's perturbation span, positive = CSET/wCSET better). wCSET degraded gradually and never became significantly worse than sLORETA, whereas CSET held up to moderate perturbation and then fell below it.

For localization error (Annex Figure 7), wCSET's error rose from `{python} deg_summary_loc_wcset_0` mm without perturbation to `{python} deg_summary_loc_wcset_100` mm at 100%, against `{python} deg_summary_ref_loc_sloreta` mm for sLORETA. It was significantly lower than sLORETA's up to `{python} deg_loc_wcset_better_end`% perturbation (`{python} deg_loc_wcset_better_d`; p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_wcset_better_p`), and never significantly higher. CSET's error stayed at `{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_lo_s`–`{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_hi_s` mm up to 60%, then rose to `{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_100` mm. It was lower than sLORETA's up to `{python} deg_loc_cset_better_end`% (`{python} deg_loc_cset_better_d`; p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_cset_better_p`), but higher from `{python} deg_loc_cset_worse_start`% on (`{python} deg_loc_cset_worse_d`; p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_cset_worse_p`).

Spatial correlation followed the same pattern (Annex Figure 8). wCSET's correlation fell from `{python} deg_summary_corr_wcset_0` to `{python} deg_summary_corr_wcset_100`, against `{python} deg_summary_ref_corr_sloreta` for sLORETA. It was significantly higher than sLORETA's up to `{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_end`% (`{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_d`; p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_p`), and its deficit at 100% was not significant (p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_wcset_worse_p`). CSET's correlation stayed at `{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_lo_s`–`{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_hi_s` up to 60%, then dropped to `{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_100`. It was higher than sLORETA's up to `{python} deg_corr_cset_better_end`% (`{python} deg_corr_cset_better_d`; p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_cset_better_p`), but lower from `{python} deg_corr_cset_worse_start`% on (`{python} deg_corr_cset_worse_d`; p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_cset_worse_p`).

### Surrogate alternatives {#sec-s1-surrogates}

```{python filename="simf_surrogate_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

DELTA_CORR = 0.1  # non-inferiority margin for spatial correlation: Cohen's smallest q [@cohen_statistical_1988] (DELTA_LOC_MM for localization error)

# Surrogate connectomes compared with the original.
surrogates = ["beltrami", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"]
conditions = ["original"] + surrogates

# Display names for the surrogate tags.
SURROGATE_LABELS = {
    "beltrami": "Beltrami (GBF)", "fused": "atlas", "fused-bin": "atlas-bin",
    "geom-atlas": "local", "geom-atlas-bin": "local-bin",
}
methods = ["cset", "wcset"]
OUTCOMES = [("localization_error", "qrp"), ("correlation", "qrp"), ("correlation", "pp")]
HIGHER_IS_BETTER = {"localization_error": False, "correlation": True}
DELTA = {"localization_error": DELTA_LOC_MM, "correlation": DELTA_CORR}

# Surrogate vs. original connectome, per method and outcome: Wilcoxon signed-rank, paired by region (mean
# over its repetitions), ties kept (Pratt), Holm across the 5 surrogates. Hodges-Lehmann shift and
# rank-biserial r, each with its 95% CI.
surr_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/surrogates")
surr_comparisons = surr_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["original"], surrogates)
surr_results = {
    (method, metric, phase): surr_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
        metric, group_by="Surrogate", comparisons=surr_comparisons, pairing_col="region",
        filters={"Method": method, "phase": phase}, correction="holm", zero_method="pratt",
        effect_sizes=("hodges_lehmann", "rank_biserial"), ci_seed=0,
    )
    for method in methods for metric, phase in OUTCOMES
}

# Read-outs oriented so that positive = surrogate better: `vs("original")` reads positive = original
# better, so the metric's direction is flipped.
surr_vs = {key: res.vs("original", higher_is_better=not HIGHER_IS_BETTER[key[1]]) for key, res in surr_results.items()}

# Non-inferiority: the surrogate is worse than the original by less than the margin, i.e. the whole
# Hodges-Lehmann CI lies above -margin.
surr_noninferior = {key: (v["hodges_lehmann_ci_low"] > -DELTA[key[1]]).to_dict() for key, v in surr_vs.items()}

# Statistics quoted in the prose (wCSET). The prose splits the surrogates in two: those that match the original
# (no significant difference and non-inferior, on localization and peak correlation) and those that significantly
# worsen localization beyond the margin. Every surrogate is non-inferior in peak correlation, and only GBF lowers
# it significantly. All checked here.
_loc_wcset = surr_vs[("wcset", "localization_error", "qrp")]
_corr_wcset_qrp = surr_vs[("wcset", "correlation", "qrp")]
_corr_wcset_pp = surr_vs[("wcset", "correlation", "pp")]
_ni_loc = surr_noninferior[("wcset", "localization_error", "qrp")]
_ni_pp = surr_noninferior[("wcset", "correlation", "pp")]
surr_match = [s_ for s_ in surrogates if _ni_loc[s_] and _ni_pp[s_]
              and not _loc_wcset.loc[s_, "significant"] and not _corr_wcset_pp.loc[s_, "significant"]]
surr_worse = [s_ for s_ in surrogates if s_ not in surr_match]
assert surr_match and surr_worse
assert all(_loc_wcset.loc[s_, "significant"] and _loc_wcset.loc[s_, "hodges_lehmann"] < 0 and not _ni_loc[s_]
           for s_ in surr_worse)
assert all(_ni_pp.values())
assert list(_corr_wcset_pp.index[_corr_wcset_pp["significant"]]) == ["beltrami"]
assert _corr_wcset_pp.loc["beltrami", "hodges_lehmann"] < 0

def _names(ss):
    labels = [SURROGATE_LABELS[s_] for s_ in ss]
    return labels[0] if len(labels) == 1 else ", ".join(labels[:-1]) + f" and {labels[-1]}"

surr_match_names, surr_worse_names = _names(surr_match), _names(surr_worse)
surr_match_p_min = f'{min(_loc_wcset.loc[surr_match, "p_corrected"].min(), _corr_wcset_pp.loc[surr_match, "p_corrected"].min()):.2f}'
# Largest deficit each matching surrogate's CI allows, as a positive number
surr_match_loc_ci = fmt_num(-_loc_wcset.loc[surr_match, "hodges_lehmann_ci_low"].min())
surr_match_pp_ci = fmt_num(-_corr_wcset_pp.loc[surr_match, "hodges_lehmann_ci_low"].min(), 2)
surr_worse_loc = " and ".join(
    f'{SURROGATE_LABELS[s_]} by {fmt_ci(_flip(_loc_wcset.loc[s_], "hodges_lehmann"), "hodges_lehmann", unit=" mm")}'
    for s_ in surr_worse)
surr_beltrami_pp = fmt_ci(_flip(_corr_wcset_pp.loc["beltrami"], "hodges_lehmann"), "hodges_lehmann", digits=2)
surr_beltrami_pp_p = fmt_p(_corr_wcset_pp.loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])
surr_pp_ci_min = fmt_num(-_corr_wcset_pp["hodges_lehmann_ci_low"].min(), 2)
corr_wcset_hl_lo_qrp, corr_wcset_hl_hi_qrp = (fmt_num(_corr_wcset_qrp["hodges_lehmann"].min(), 2),
                                              fmt_num(_corr_wcset_qrp["hodges_lehmann"].max(), 2))

# CSET: the Laplace-Beltrami surrogate markedly worsens localization; every other significant difference
# is a small deficit (largest quoted per metric, as a positive number).
_cset_beltrami = surr_vs[("cset", "localization_error", "qrp")].loc["beltrami"]
assert _cset_beltrami["hodges_lehmann"] < 0 and _cset_beltrami["significant"]
cset_beltrami_loc_hl = fmt_ci(_flip(_cset_beltrami, "hodges_lehmann"), "hodges_lehmann", unit=" mm")
_cset_other = {
    (metric, s): v.loc[s, "hodges_lehmann"]
    for (method, metric, phase), v in surr_vs.items() if method == "cset"
    for s in surrogates
    if v.loc[s, "significant"] and (metric, s) != ("localization_error", "beltrami")
}
assert all(d < 0 for d in _cset_other.values())
cset_other_loc_max = fmt_num(-min([d for (m, _), d in _cset_other.items() if m == "localization_error"], default=0))
cset_other_corr_max = fmt_num(-min([d for (m, _), d in _cset_other.items() if m == "correlation"], default=0), 2)

# dSPM's and sLORETA's benchmark reference lines, taken from the Study I results above and summarized
# like the boxes they are drawn over: mean over repetitions per region, median across regions.
# Correlation: the per-region curves of the Study I figure (corr_collapsed) at the median qrp/peak time.
_ref_methods = ["dspm", "sloreta"]
surr_ref_loc = (simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp", "Method": _ref_methods})
                .groupby(["Method", "region"])["Value"].mean().groupby("Method").median().to_dict())
surr_ref_corr = {
    phase: corr_collapsed[(corr_collapsed["times"] == t) & corr_collapsed["Method"].isin(_ref_methods)]
           .groupby("Method")["Value"].median().to_dict()
    for phase, t in phase_times.items()
}

# wCSET's correlation at the peak with each surrogate, relative to dSPM's and sLORETA's references.
_wcset_pp = (surr_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation", filters={"Method": "wcset", "phase": "pp"})
             .groupby(["Surrogate", "region"])["Value"].mean().groupby("Surrogate").median())
_ratios = [_wcset_pp[s] / surr_ref_corr["pp"][m] for s in surrogates for m in _ref_methods]
corr_wcset_ref_ratio_lo, corr_wcset_ref_ratio_hi = fmt_num(min(_ratios), 1), fmt_num(max(_ratios), 1)
```

We replaced the true connectome with the dMRI-free surrogates of @sec-connectome, keeping wCSET's hyperparameters unchanged (@fig-surrogate; Hodges–Lehmann shifts, positive = surrogate better). With the `{python} surr_match_names` surrogates, wCSET performed as well as with the true connectome. Neither its localization error nor its spatial correlation at the peak differed significantly (all p_corrected ≥ `{python} surr_match_p_min`), and every CI excluded a deficit as large as the non-inferiority margins (at most `{python} surr_match_loc_ci` mm and Δr = `{python} surr_match_pp_ci`, against margins of 5 mm and 0.1). The other surrogates significantly worsened its localization, and their CIs extended beyond the 5 mm margin: `{python} surr_worse_loc`. With the Beltrami surrogate (GBF), its spatial correlation at the peak was also lower, by Δr = `{python} surr_beltrami_pp` (p_corrected `{python} surr_beltrami_pp_p`). This loss remained well within the margin, as for every surrogate (largest deficit within the CIs: Δr = `{python} surr_pp_ci_min`), and wCSET's correlation at the peak stayed `{python} corr_wcset_ref_ratio_lo`–`{python} corr_wcset_ref_ratio_hi` times that of dSPM and sLORETA with every surrogate. At the quarter rising phase, before activity spreads, the surrogates changed spatial correlation little (Δr = `{python} corr_wcset_hl_lo_qrp` to `{python} corr_wcset_hl_hi_qrp`; Annex Figure 10).

CSET changed little: with most surrogates, differences were either not significant or small deficits (at most `{python} cset_other_loc_max` mm in localization error and Δr = `{python} cset_other_corr_max` in spatial correlation). The exception was the Laplace-Beltrami surrogate (GBF), which worsened its localization by `{python} cset_beltrami_loc_hl`. Full CSET results are in Annex Figure 9.

```{python filename="simf_surrogate_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
```
